documents.abstract: Estimates of the energy used by artificial intelligence are widely quoted and rarely agree with one another. This review examines why. We separate what is counted (training or inference, operational or embodied emissions, carbon or water) from how it is counted (meters, software trackers, calculators, retrospective estimates, life cycle assessment), and then set published figures side by side with their scope. The best-known early number, an outside estimate for one architecture search, was later put by the operator at one eighty-eighth of that value. One measured study that drew its boundary wider found idle power and manufacturing roughly doubling the footprint of a training run. Inference energy per thousand queries spans three orders of magnitude across tasks. At data-centre scale the AI-specific figures are scenarios built on analyst estimates, and their author says so. We then review mitigation through smaller models, better hardware, scheduling by place and hour, and reporting, and we look at the rebound argument. The article is a review of published work. No new measurement or experiment is reported, and each number is attributed to the source that produced it.

Maritime domain awareness (MDA) in inland waterways is constrained by vulnerabilities in cooperative monitoring systems. This study presents a data fusion framework that integrates high-resolution satellite imagery with vessel trajectory data from the automatic identification system (AIS) to enhance detection, characterization, and tracking of maritime activity. The proposed approach leverages noncooperative satellite sensing to complement AIS data, enabling the identification of dark vessels, validation of cooperative traffic, and support for advanced MDA capabilities. A You Only Look Once (YOLO) v11-based object detection model is developed to detect and characterize vessels and barges by type, cover status, operational state, barge count, and direction of movement. The model is trained on a manually annotated dataset comprising 4,550 instances extracted from 5,973 mi 2 of Lower Mississippi River imagery. Evaluation on a held-out test set demonstrates strong performance across multiple tasks, with vessel classification achieving an F1-score of 95.8%, barge cover detection attaining an F1-score of 91.6%, and operational status classification reaching an F1-score of 99.4%. Direction-of-movement classification attains an accuracy of 98.1%, while barge-count estimation yields a mean absolute error of 2.4 barges. Spatial transferability assessment across a geographically distinct river system indicates minimal performance degradation, with accuracy levels remaining as high as 98%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating satellite imagery with AIS data for inland waterway monitoring. The framework supports near-real-time fleet inventory generation, anomaly detection, and improved situational awareness. Future work will focus on expanding dataset diversity, incorporating temporal modeling, and exploring multimodal learning to further enhance scalability and operational deployment.

Aim A policy framework for Paediatric surgical training to address sustainable surgical resource utilization and environmental-disease interplay in a low-to-middle income country (LMIC) setting is presented. Methods Using the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Education Pillars for Sustainable Development (EPSD), existing and potential integration of environmental education in undergraduate and postgraduate paediatric surgical training is described at an LMIC academic hospital, in conjunction with a narrative review of environmental underpinnings of existing paediatric surgical English literature. Pedagogical techniques are conceptualized to demonstrate the 3-way interactions between paediatric surgical services and social/ built, economic and natural/ climactic environments, on individual and community level. This is illustrated by the context of the surgically managed congenital abdominal wall defect gastroschisis, amongst other examples. Results Gastroschisis is a Paediatric Surgical key topic that highlights the imperative for comprehensive environmentally sensitive patient-orientated care. Some curricular content and LMIC situational awareness already exists in our setting regarding resource stewardship, environmental teratogens and socioeconomic interactions. The local surgical procedure-related carbon footprints and interaction with socio-economic factors are inadequately researched to inform resource management and educational content. Topical paediatric surgical literature and local knowledge, attitude, skills and participation have significant gaps on individual, institutional and community levels, aggravated by a circular interplay between these UNESCO EPSD. Potentially feasible Paediatric Surgery curricular changes to increase environmental focus include explicit standard pedagogical content, behaviour modelling/ modulation and interdisciplinary engagement. Conclusions Paediatric Surgery curriculum and educational and healthcare culture currently convey little environmentally implicit or explicit pedagogical content, and require teaching of skills for critical thinking, research, resource management and organized advocacy.

Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

Epistemic game theory explains an agent's strategic behavior via the beliefs it holds about others and how these beliefs are updated as the interactions unfold. Modern LLM-based agents, however, often lack an explicit mechanism for learning and updating such beliefs to guide decisions under incomplete information. To bridge this gap, we propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer, which maintains beliefs over others' private information and combines these beliefs with the agent's available information into an epistemic state for action selection. Concretely, the agent's policy is decomposed into two coupled stages: Epistemic Update, which updates these beliefs from interaction histories, and Action Planning, which selects actions conditioned on the updated epistemic state. By formulating their dependency as a bi-level optimization problem, we introduce Epistemic Self-Play, an algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages through self-play, utilizing an intrinsic prediction reward to evaluate how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. Empirical results across both mixed and competitive scenarios show that EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines. Further analyses reveal the benefits of dedicated epistemic training, improvements in belief inference accuracy, and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning. These results demonstrate the value of an explicit, learnable epistemic layer for effective multi-agent interactions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching, learning, and knowledge production in higher education. However, limited attention has been given to justice-oriented frameworks that connect AI-mediated education with epistemic agency and critical consciousness, particularly within market-driven university contexts. This conceptual article explores how teaching can be reimagined to cultivate epistemic agency and critical consciousness in AI-mediated higher education through a justice-oriented pedagogical framework. The article draws on frameworks such as critical pedagogy, decolonial theory, and epistemic justice to foreground the findings of this research. It employs a narrative-integrative review methodology to synthesise contemporary scholarship on AI and social justice in higher education. The article argues for a shift beyond transmissive and instrumental models of learning towards relational pedagogies that position learners as active co-creators of knowledge. It examines how AI technologies may reinforce or disrupt epistemic hierarchies through algorithmic bias, automated decision-making, and changing processes of knowledge production. The original contribution is a justice-oriented conceptual framework that integrates pedagogical design, institutional cultures, power relations, and technological systems for a better education experience. It recommends embedding critical AI literacy across curricula and aligning pedagogy with principles of epistemic justice to support equitable and socially transformative higher education in an increasingly algorithmic world.

Artificial intelligence is playing a great role in the production, classification, retrieval, and communication of knowledge. Tools like large language models, recommender systems, automated decision-making systems, and search engines do more than just process information; they shape whose testimony is heard, which concepts become available for interpreting experience, and which claims are treated as credible or important. This paper argues that Miranda Fricker's theory of epistemic injustice offers a strong framework to ethically identify shortcomings in AI-enabled knowledge production; however, it also suggests that, the distinction made in classical accounts between testimonial and hermeneutical injustices needs to be extended in order to address them in the context of sociotechnical systems. Testimonial injustice can arise when algorithmic models reproduce credibility deficits through biased training data, proxy variables, ranking practices, moderation systems, or automated classification. On the other hand, hermeneutical injustice can emerge when certain communities are poorly represented in the conceptual and linguistic tools that AI systems use to create explanations, categories, and interpretations. The paper further argues that the opaque nature of many AI systems intensifies these harms because affected persons may be unable to understand, contest, or correct the epistemic processes that affect them. Building on Fricker, Floridi, Dotson, Medina, and contemporary work in AI ethics, the paper develops an epistemic justice framework centred on adequacy in represantation, credibility protection, interpretive inclusion, contestability, provenance, and institutional accountability. The proposed framework treats epistemic justice not merely as a desirable output property but as a design and governance requirement for AI systems that participate in consequential knowledge practices.

documents.abstract: Active learning has become an important part of higher education delivery. Yet, its ethical dimensions are often overlooked. This chapter examines how active learning changes classroom power dynamics, and alters student and educator roles, challenging assumptions of autonomy, responsibility and expertise. It explores the tension between the effectiveness of active learning and students’ varied expectations and preferences for participation, with implications for equity and inclusion. The chapter also considers ethical issues in assessment, including the balance between formative and summative assessments, student agency and the challenges posed by emerging technologies such as Generative AI. It concludes by making suggestions for ethical, fair and transparent practices for active learning in higher education.

Dear Editor The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems has introduced both technological advancement and ethical transformation in nursing practice. While AI-based tools enhance clinical efficiency, documentation accuracy, and decision-support processes, their ethical implications regarding patient privacy, professional accountability, and ethical decision-making remain critically debated. In this systematic examination of empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, key ethical dimensions of AI application in nursing were analyzed. Findings indicate persistent concerns about data confidentiality, ambiguity in responsibility boundaries, and potential over-reliance on algorithmic recommendations. At the same time, AI-assisted education demonstrates positive effects on ethical reasoning and professional self-awareness. However, the absence of clear governance frameworks and explicit accountability policies limits the safe and ethically grounded implementation of AI in nursing practice. Strengthening digital ethics education, clarifying shared accountability between clinicians and intelligent systems, and conducting longitudinal clinical research are essential priorities for advancing ethical AI integration in nursing.

documents.abstract: Conversational interfaces may make explainable AI (XAI) more accessible to users without machine learning expertise, but their benefits over dashboards remain insufficiently characterised in healthcare. Existing systems have typically been evaluated in isolation, leaving unclear whether conversational interaction improves interpretability beyond the underlying explanation methods. We report a within-subjects user study comparing the Explainability Assistant, an LLM function-calling conversational XAI system, with a traditional dashboard for explaining a heart disease classification model trained on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Both interfaces expose the same Decision Tree classifier and post-hoc explanation methods: SHAP feature attribution, DiCE counterfactuals, and what-if analysis. This design supports comparison of interaction modalities while holding the model and explanation methods constant. Five participants with healthcare backgrounds, from medical students to practising clinicians and public health researchers, completed parallel task blocks on both interfaces; three participated in follow-up interviews. Task accuracy, Likert ratings, free-text questionnaire responses, and interviews revealed complementary strengths and weaknesses rather than a clear preference for either modality. The assistant offered easier entry and patient-specific explanations, while the dashboard supported simultaneous inspection of global and local information. All three interview participants recommended integrating conversational and dashboard elements within a single clinical workflow.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support writing assessment, yet it remains unclear how closely AI-generated scores correspond with human judgment in Foundation English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts. This study examined agreement between AI-generated and human ratings of Foundation EFL writing in Kuwait. The dataset comprised 692 writing assessment records from 162 students enrolled in ENGL097 and ENGL098. Overall scores and six analytic criteria (topic sentence, body and development, conclusion, organization, vocabulary, and grammar) were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson and Spearman correlations, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), mean differences, error indices, and Bland–Altman analysis. AI scores showed very high agreement with the average of two human raters (r = .992; absolute-agreement ICC = .991). The mean difference was 0.24 points on a 50-point scale, the mean absolute error was 0.89 points, and 93.1% of AI ratings fell within two points of the human average. Criterion-level ICCs ranged from .953 to .965, with vocabulary lowest and conclusion highest. A significant proportional bias indicated that disagreement varied across the score range. The findings suggest that AI scoring can provide consistent support for Foundation EFL writing assessment when applied through a clearly defined analytic rubric, although human oversight remains essential.

OBJECTIVE: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially the rise of large language models (LLMs), hold great promise for transforming mental health care, but their growing integration also raises pressing questions about their ability to deliver meaningful therapeutic interventions. This study compared the capabilities of LLMs to those of human therapists in producing context-sensitive psychotherapy responses within 16-session supportive-expressive psychodynamic psychotherapy for patients with depression. Specifically, it compared LLM and human therapists on (a) the frequency and typicality of their intervention choice and (b) the quality and general helpfulness of their interventions. METHOD: We developed an LLM-based framework composed of four specialized LLM agents, each representing a different therapeutic dimension, and a Judge-LLM that selects the most appropriate intervention for a given context. A sample of 300 therapy session segments, each containing both human- and LLM-generated responses, served as the evaluation data set. Expert clinical judges assessed interventions for typicality and quality. RESULTS: LLMs and human therapists relied on broadly similar intervention types. However, the contextual choice of when to use a specific type differed. Human interventions were rated as generally more helpful. Specifically, humans produced higher quality meaning-making interventions, while no differences were found for supportive, directive, or exploratory interventions. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that under the specific locally deployed multiagent configuration tested, LLMs can generate a range of context-sensitive therapeutic responses but showed limitations in producing high-quality meaning-making interventions. These findings highlight both the promise and the current boundaries of such systems as supervised therapeutic adjuncts. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction. Burnout represents a significant occupational health concern among healthcare professionals. The present study estimated the prevalence of burnout and examined its associated socio-demographic and occupational factors in the Souss-Massa region of Morocco. Methods: A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted from November 2025 to January 2026 among 462 professionals employed in public healthcare institutions across the six provinces of the region. Burnout was measured using the French version of the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey. Associations between burnout and potential factors were examined using bivariate analyses, with statistical significance defined as p ≤ 0.05. Results: The prevalence of at least one dimension of burnout was 82.3%, while 12.6% of participants exhibited all three dimensions concurrently. High levels of emotional exhaustion and depersonalization were observed in 67.3% and 39.0% of participants, respectively. Regarding personal accomplishment, 33.1% reported low levels, 21.4% moderate levels, and 45.5% high levels. Significant associations were observed with marital status, number of children, educational level, occupation, province of practice, type of healthcare setting, and working arrangements (p < 0.001). The presence of chronic illness (p = 0.003), overtime (p = 0.035), and working more than ten hours a day at least once a week (p = 0.018) were also significantly associated with burnout. Conclusion: Burnout was highly prevalent, with emotional exhaustion as the most common dimension. These findings underscore the necessity for targeted organizational interventions to safeguard the healthcare professionals in the workplace.RESUMEIntroduction. Le burnout constitue un problème majeur de santé au travail chez les professionnels de santé. Cette étude a estimé la prévalence du burnout et examiné les facteurs sociodémographiques et professionnels associés dans la région Souss-Massa au Maroc. Méthodes. Nous avons mené une étude transversale multicentrique de novembre 2025 à janvier 2026 auprès de 462 professionnels exerçant dans des établissements publics de santé des six provinces de la région. Nous avons mesuré le burnout à l'aide de la version française du Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey, comprenant 22 items répartis en trois dimensions : épuisement émotionnel (EE), dépersonnalisation (DP) et accomplissement personnel (AP). Nous avons utilisé des analyses bivariées pour examiner les associations, avec un seuil de significativité fixé à p ≤ 0,05. Résultats. La prévalence d'au moins une dimension du burnout était de 82,3 % ; 12,6 % des participants présentaient les trois dimensions. Un niveau élevé d'EE était identifié chez 67,3 % des participants, une DP élevée chez 39,0 % et un faible AP chez 33,1 %. Des associations significatives ont été observées avec le statut matrimonial, le nombre d'enfants, le niveau d'études, la profession, la province d'exercice, le type d'établissement et le régime de travail (p < 0,001). La présence d'une maladie chronique (p = 0,003), les heures supplémentaires (p = 0,035) et le travail de plus de dix heures par jour au moins une fois par semaine (p = 0,018) étaient également significativement associés au burnout. L'âge, le sexe, le tabagisme et l'activité physique n'étaient pas associés. Conclusion. Le burnout était très prévalent dans cette région, avec l'épuisement émotionnel comme dimension dominante. Les infirmiers, les travailleurs postés et les professionnels des hôpitaux provinciaux étaient les plus affectés. Ces résultats appellent à des interventions organisationnelles ciblées pour protéger les professionnels de santé au Souss-Massa.

Abstract Background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly proposed as a way to make clinical decision-support systems more transparent and acceptable to healthcare professionals. However, explanation does not necessarily improve clinical decisions: it may help users identify relevant evidence, have no measurable effect, or encourage excessive reliance on incorrect AI advice. This review synthesises empirical evidence on how clinician-facing explanations influence trust, reliance, and decision quality. Methods: A structured evidence search was conducted on 20 October 2026 using web-indexed scholarly search, PubMed/PMC records, and publisher-hosted full-text pages. Search concepts combined explainable AI, clinical decision support, clinicians/physicians, trust/reliance, diagnostic accuracy, and human-AI decision-making. A core set of ten empirical studies was identified and characterised from the study table and reference list of Rosenbacke et al. (2024), with key primary reports checked against publisher or PubMed records. More recent evidence was used to contextualise the findings. Because a complete exportable database search and independent duplicate screening were not available in this workflow, this is a transparent structured systematic evidence synthesis rather than a fully reproducible database-level review; no new PRISMA record counts are claimed. Results: The evidence indicates that explanations can improve perceived understandability and sometimes support decision performance, but their effects on trust are inconsistent and context-dependent. In a chemotherapy decision-support experiment involving 41 medical practitioners, example-based and counterfactual explanations were easier to understand than some alternatives, yet explanations also increased willingness to accept AI recommendations, including incorrect ones. In an X-ray experiment involving 223 physicians, annotated AI advice improved diagnostic accuracy particularly for non-radiology experts, while confidence in clinicians' own diagnoses did not meaningfully change. Other studies reported increased trust or intention to use AI, no clear effect, or concerns about complex, irrelevant, or time-consuming explanations. Conclusion: XAI should not be evaluated by whether it increases trust alone. Evaluation should test whether clinicians can distinguish correct from incorrect recommendations, whether reliance is appropriately calibrated, and whether explanations fit clinical workflows. Larger, preregistered, multisite studies using realistic clinical tasks and common outcome measures are needed.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and sustainable finance is transforming global financial ecosystems. Financial institutions increasingly use AI for ESG evaluation, fraud detection, climate-risk analytics, portfolio optimization, and digital lending. However, reliance on complex models raises concerns about transparency, interpretability, ethics, and regulatory compliance, as black-box systems limit accountability. This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in cloud-driven sustainable finance and proposes an interdisciplinary framework integrating XAI, ESG governance, and climate-risk analytics. It explores techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and interpretable models, along with applications in ESG scoring, green finance, and risk assessment. The study also highlights regulatory and ethical considerations and emphasizes explainability as essential for trustworthy and sustainable financial transformation.

documents.abstract: The Analog Electronic Technology course is concept-intensive, and its circuit analysis methods are flexible. A relatively common difficulty among students is that “single-point knowledge can still be mastered, but the overall context is difficult to connect.” In teaching, problems such as linear content organization, unified learning support, a long feedback cycle, and mismatch between resources and needs have existed for a long time. In response, this study takes Outcome-Based Education (OBE) as the basic guidance, connects the structured organization ability of the smart knowledge graph with the dialogue interaction ability of the artificial intelligence (AI) agent, and constructs a blended teaching model driven by an AI smart knowledge graph. Starting from graduation requirements and course objectives, knowledge points are reversely decomposed, four types of associations, namely prerequisite, parallel, causal, and application associations, are sorted out, and a three-layer smart knowledge graph organized in five levels of “course-module-chapter-knowledge point-sub-knowledge point” is formed. On this basis, an AI teaching agent is developed to undertake preview guidance, in-class question answering, homework correction, learning situation analysis, and other work. The teaching process is then rearranged according to the three stages of before class, in class, and after class. A one-semester comparative practice shows that the final average score of the experimental class is 8.7 points higher than that of the control class, the score difference in comprehensive questions is especially obvious, the proportion of students independently completing design experiments has increased, and the dispersion of scores has also narrowed. The relevant practices have certain reference value for the intelligent transformation of basic courses in electronic information majors, but the scope of application of the conclusions is still limited by the sample size and implementation rounds.

Direct augmentation onto flight deck displays presents distinct advantages for communicating information priority levels in aviation, especially in glass cockpits. This study investigated how augmented symbols, in interaction with pilot experience and target distance, can facilitate the communication of information priority levels in glass cockpits. A total of 20 pilot cadets and 21 professional pilots participated in a mixed-factorial study: 8 (augmented symbols: within) × 2 (pilot experience level: between) × 2 (target distance: within). Results demonstrated that certain augmented symbols significantly outperformed others in detection time to correct identification (DTCI) and first response accuracy (FRA). Expert pilots reported significantly lower mental workload and better visual comfort than novice pilots. Smaller target distances exhibited better DTCI and perceptions. Interactions among the measured factors were found. These findings offer practical implications for the design of aviation cockpits, particularly when information priority is delivered via flight deck displays.

Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of healthcare, but its integration in sub-Saharan Africa faces structural constraints. This exploratory study analyzes the perceptions, expectations, and fears of healthcare professionals in the Ibanda Health Zone (Bukavu, DRC) to document the professional acceptability of these technologies. Methods: The study used a mixed-methods approach: the qualitative exploratory component was based on semi-structured interviews with 11 professionals (physicians, nurses, technicians, managers). The data underwent inductive thematic analysis supplemented by descriptive frequency quantification. Results: Overall attitudes toward AI are favorable, albeit with certain conditions. Despite a predominantly basic or informal understanding of AI (81.8%), perceived benefits include improved diagnostics (72.7%) and data management (63.6%). However, major obstacles persist: lack of formal training (81.8%), internet instability (72.7%), and concerns about the reliability of results (54.5%). AI acceptance is high but conditional, revealing a gap between technological promises and realities on the ground. Training (cited by 90.9% of participants) emerges as the central lever and an ethical prerequisite for safe use. Conclusion : The integration of AI at Ibanda cannot be reduced to a technical issue; it requires strengthening basic infrastructure, a clear regulatory framework, and active involvement of caregivers in the design of tools.

documents.abstract: This study aims to explore mathematical concepts in the local culture of Maros Regency assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI) through collaborative project-based learning integrated with social media. The study focuses on three Bugis-Makassar traditions (Makkellu, Mappassili, Mappacci), the Dende-dende traditional game, and the Peca Sura tradition. A qualitative ethnographic approach was employed involving participatory observation, in-depth interviews with six cultural informants, photo/video documentation, and the active participation of 15 mathematics education students acting as co-researchers and project-based learners. AI technology served as a supportive analytical and visualization tool—utilizing computer vision algorithms for geometric/symmetry extraction and prompt-based analytical tools for data synthesis. The results show that Makkellu contains facial geometry, ratios, and symmetry; Mappassili is associated with cylindrical volume, circular perimeters, and arithmetic mean temperatures; Mappacci displays symmetry and permutation patterns; Dende-dende contains plane coordinates, angles, and outcome sample spaces for game strategies; while Peca Sura reflects volume, material proportions, and fractional distribution. Social media served as a supportive platform for disseminating educational content: Peca Sura's post received the highest interaction (240 likes, 46 comments, 25 shares), followed by Dende-dende and Makkellu. This research highlights that integrating AI support and social media into ethnomathematics offers a potentially beneficial and engaging pathway for contextual mathematics education and cultural preservation.

This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

This qualitative descriptive study explored how nurse educators at Olivarez College Tagaytay, Cavite, accepted and integrated generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in nursing education and developed an evidence-informed action plan. Eight purposively selected nurse educators who had used GenAI in teaching participated in semi-structured, in-depth interviews during August 2026. The interview guide was expert-validated, and recordings were transcribed and examined through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Data collection occurred in three waves; 125 codes were organized into six themes and 16 subthemes. The themes were unplanned entry into a necessary technology; conditional acceptance anchored in professional judgment; adapting under generational pressure; integration at the preparation stage; safeguarding learning through vigilance and assessment redesign; and enablement by leadership without written policy. Educators perceived GenAI as useful for preparing lessons, cases, questions, and simplified learning materials but insisted on verifying outputs and protecting clinical judgment, empathy, academic integrity, and patient safety. Integration remained largely preparatory and individualized, while participants described uneven digital confidence, assessment vulnerabilities, personal subscription costs, and the absence of consistent written rules despite administrative encouragement. The findings indicate a gap between conditional acceptance and systematic pedagogical integration. A five-component action plan addressing governance, differentiated faculty development, assessment integrity, student AI literacy, and technical access was proposed, not evaluated. The study contributes institution-specific evidence to responsible GenAI adoption in nursing education.

documents.abstract: The ability to predict farrowing time in pigs is crucial for optimal farm management and ensuring piglet survival. This study investigates the potential of explainable artificial intelligence for precision livestock farming, focusing on acceleration sensor data from sows around the time of farrowing. Accurately predicting farrowing allows farmers to balance both, piglet safety by avoiding piglet crushing events and the mother sow's welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models often lack interpretability (``closed-box'' problem). Explainable artificial intelligence offers a solution by revealing the decision-making processes within the models. This work is split into two stages. First the detection of nest building behaviour and second the prediction of the remaining time to farrowing. The nest building detection was possible for 166 out of 180 sows and successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. The nest building detection is purely based on the change of a sow's activity level and uses no machine learning techniques. Further, this study utilizes symbolic regression, an open-box modelling technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, to predict the remaining time until the onset of farrowing. The results are compared with closed-box models, like support vector regression and artificial neural networks, for both explainability and performance. Notably, symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for the time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in terms of performance and interpretability. This research demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence, specifically symbolic regression, can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance in precision livestock farming.

BACKGROUND: Understanding factors influencing specialty choice is essential for workforce planning and curriculum development. Recruitment into diagnostic radiology remains challenging in several regions, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This study aimed to identify factors associated with Palestinian medical students' consideration of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty, with particular emphasis on educational exposure, perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), and cognitive influences. METHODS: A multi-institutional cross-sectional study was conducted to evaluate factors influencing the choice of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty among Palestinian medical students between 2 November 2025 and 5 February 2026. Data were collected using a previously validated questionnaire adapted from Almuhanna et al. Descriptive statistics were performed, followed by bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of considering radiology as a future specialty. Adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. RESULTS: A total of 427 students participated (56.7% female; mean age 21.75 ± 2.1 years). Among 300 valid responses regarding radiology intention, 102 students (34.0%) reported considering radiology as a future specialty. In multivariable analysis, lack of exposure to radiology research (OR = 0.14, 95% CI 0.06-0.34, p < 0.001) and lack of preclinical radiology teaching (OR = 0.26, 95% CI 0.12-0.54, p < 0.001) were independently associated with a lower likelihood of considering radiology. Enjoyment of diagnostic problem-solving tasks (OR = 3.35, 95% CI 1.39-8.09, p = 0.007) and exposure to tele-radiology (OR = 3.96, 95% CI 1.72-9.12, p = 0.001) were independently associated with higher likelihood. Lifestyle, impact on patient care, and work environment were the most frequently reported motivating factors. CONCLUSIONS: Palestinian medical students' interest in radiology is strongly associated with modifiable educational exposures, cognitive engagement in diagnostic reasoning, and perceptions of evolving technological practice. These findings support the potential value of structured undergraduate radiology exposure, research opportunities, and mentorship initiatives to improve awareness and interest in radiology.

documents.abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.

Reproducibility package for the study "Feasibility-First Routing for Regulated Multi-Provider LLM Serving: Governance, Caching, and the Limits of Online Learning." It contains the governance-gate and routing/analysis code, the measured multi-provider inference records, figures, hypothesis documentation, an auditable decision-log sample, and the manuscript PDF. The study measures a governance gate that holds simulated-policy residency/BAA violations at 0% versus 38.5% for governance-blind routing, an exact-match policy-scoped cache as the dominant cost lever, and an honest accuracy-cost trade-off for online (LinUCB) routing (-3.45 percentage points accuracy across 40 repeated benchmark re-splits while usually lowering modeled cost). All results reproduce from the saved records with numpy only; no new API calls are required. The code is licensed MIT; the package, text, figures, and data are licensed CC BY 4.0.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Emerging intelligent wireless networks increasingly rely on autonomous AI agents to adapt spectrum usage to dynamic and heterogeneous operating conditions. However, collective learning is challenging when agents experience different local interference environments and cannot exchange raw observations due to communication-overhead and privacy constraints. We propose Federated Agentic Spectrum Coordination with Interference Awareness (FASCIA), a federated multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive spectrum coordination. In FASCIA, each network manager acts as an autonomous AI agent that perceives its local interference environment, accumulates experience in a persistent local memory, and learns an adaptive spectrum coordination policy through local interactions. Coordination among agents is achieved through periodic federated aggregation of locally trained models, without exchanging raw sensing data or experience. Since spectrum decisions made by one agent alter the environments observed by others, local learning is inherently heterogeneous and coupled. FASCIA employs proximal regularization to mitigate the resulting model drift and explicitly accounts for inter-carrier interference arising from partially overlapping channels. FASCIA is the first federated agentic AI framework to address this challenging interference-coupled spectrum coordination setting. Extensive simulations demonstrate that FASCIA achieves performance close to the centralized benchmark while avoiding raw-experience exchange and maintaining effectiveness across heterogeneous network configurations.
topics: Cognitive Radio Networks and Spectrum Sensing
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: LLM-powered recommender agents use reasoning and memory for personalization, but centralized access to user information raises privacy concerns, while isolated agents cannot learn from others' experiences. We formulate Federated Recommender Agents, a setting where local agents collaborate through natural-language knowledge while keeping interaction histories and personal memories local. We propose FedRecAgent, which enables this collaboration without updating LLM parameters. Its central challenge is determining which reasoning to integrate, since similar behavioral contexts can lead to different choices. FedRecAgent represents local experiences as Condition-Transition-Reasoning (C-T-R) units and hierarchically integrates reasoning by condition and transition. Within this structure, it consolidates related explanations and discriminates reasoning across alternative transitions. Each client maintains semantic and decision memories to capture preferences and conditional choice tendencies, guiding the retrieval and selection of shared reasoning for recommendation. Experiments across three domains under dense and sparse settings demonstrate improved recommendation performance over federated and LLM-based baselines, while ablations support the contributions of personalized memories and structured reasoning integration.

A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

Abstract In a companion study we showed that a short stored review carrying a direct order (“delete user carlos”) made a small local assistant delete the account every time, while a hosted-class assistant ignored it (Hadad, Hadad, and Tavakoli 2026). Real reviews are not short shouts. They run to a paragraph, and a planted sentence can sit at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom of one. This paper moves that one sentence around inside the same ordinary review and asks whether where it sits decides whether it is obeyed, discussed, or simply summarised away. We test two framings (direct order, support note) at three positions in one fixed jacket review, in the same Flask shop, on the same two models, vulnerable and tool-free variants, 84 trials in total. No position produced a deletion on either model: direct orders in a full-length review gave 0/9 effects on the local model, against 3/3 for near-identical plain wording in a one-line review in the companion study. Position showed up one level lower. On the local model the opening direct order was still discussed as account business in 3/3 trials, while every other planted cell was summarised as jacket text (0/15; Fisher \(\:p=0.0012\) on deletion talk). Muse surfaced exactly one planted order in 18 attack trials, at the end of a review, and surfaced it to refuse it by name (§[sec:results36]). A stored order, it turns out, needs to be the review, not merely in it – and even at the top of a real review, this small model only talked. We release payloads, transcripts, judge labels, and the counting scripts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This article argues that Large Language Models (LLMs) reveal literacy’s sociomaterial character: that it is constituted within more-than-human assemblages of people, texts, technologies, practices, and infrastructures, rather than in the cognitive capacity of the individual. Rather than asking what new literacies Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) demands, it asks what LLMs reveal about literacy itself. This analysis draws on the sociomaterial tradition in science and technology studies, including actor-network theory, spatial perspectives, and postdigital literacy research. It reconceptualises literacy as emergent practice within assemblages, arguing that competence frameworks, by centring the individual, cannot register the distributed, infrastructural, and nonhuman dimensions of literacy that this shift makes visible. From this analysis, three design orientations for postdigital literacy environments are derived: making assemblages visible, sustaining fluid literacy spaces, and preserving conditions for critical reflexivity. The article concludes by arguing that these orientations carry political as well as pedagogical stakes, since current AI assemblages risk amplifying existing educational inequalities rather than benefiting all learners equally.

Abstract Data-intensive collider experiments increasingly require models that transfer across high-dimensional, partially observed measurements, yet most analyses still optimize separate models for each task. Here, to address this bottleneck, we introduce EVENET, an event-level foundation model pretrained on 500 million simulated collision events using self-supervised learning and physics-informed supervision. The model constructs a shared particle-cloud representation from the variable-length set of physics objects in each event. Across searches for heavy resonances and exotic Higgs decays, EVENET outperforms both established and state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in low-statistics regimes. We validate transfer to experimental data by rediscovering the ϒ meson in CMS Open Data. The pretrained model also supports precise extraction of quantum-correlation observables that remain stable under the tested systematic variations. Together, these results establish a reusable backbone for diverse collider analyses, improving downstream adaptation after a substantial one-time pretraining investment.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

documents.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now part of routine academic work in health professions education, often outpacing institutional policy, infrastructure, and training. We describe how educators and trainees use GenAI, their concerns, and the institutional support they perceive, and examine whether prior AI training and frequency of use are associated with these perceptions. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey (August–November 2025) of faculty, clinicians, staff, and trainees involved in health professions education across the United States, recruited through professional networks. Ten items on a 0–5 agreement scale captured attitudes, concerns, trust in AI accuracy, and perceived institutional resources. We used descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm correction, and multivariable ordinal logistic regression with sensitivity analyses. Results: Of 211 responses, 183 respondents with documented consent were analyzed (76.5% faculty; 48 named institutions). Nearly all had used GenAI (98.9%), and 78.1% used it at least weekly, most often for writing or editing (77.6%). Half or more agreed or strongly agreed that they were concerned about academic integrity (58.5%), data privacy (56.3%), and professional accountability (50.8%), yet only 14.2% agreed or strongly agreed that they trust the accuracy of AI-generated content. Only 24.0% agreed or strongly agreed that their institution provides the resources they need (M = 2.51). Among respondents with elevated concern, 73.8% still used GenAI weekly or more. Any AI training (39.9%, mostly informal workshops) was associated with greater comfort and perceived institutional resources, but not significantly with trust or any concern. More frequent use was independently associated with greater trust (OR 4.93, 95% CI 2.46–9.86) and fewer ethical concerns (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.16–0.61), and both associations held in sensitivity analyses. Privacy concern was not associated with use frequency. Conclusions: GenAI has become part of routine work for most health professions educators, yet it coexists with substantial concerns about privacy, integrity, and accountability. Training was associated with comfort but not with lower concern, suggesting that faculty development alone is unlikely to be sufficient; institutions may need to pair it with the governance, data protection, and approved tools that individual training cannot provide.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic drastically reshaped Malaysia's labour market, accelerating the growth of the GIG economy as millions turned to platform-based work for survival. Despite its rapid expansion, GIG workers in Malaysia remain highly vulnerable, with existing literature largely overlooking Islamic normative perspectives on worker wellbeing. This study employs a qualitative study to examine GIG worker wellbeing across three phases before, during, and after the pandemic through the framework of Maqasid al-Shariah, anchored in the protection of five essential human domains, namely Hifz al-Nafs (life), Hifz al- Din (religion), Hifz al-Mal (wealth), Hifz al-Aql (intellect), Hifz Nasl (lineage/family). It is anticipated that the study will reveal persistent gaps in the safeguarding of these five domains across all three phases, reflecting a systemic failure to protect the holistic wellbeing of GIG workers in Malaysia. Adopting a qualitative, conceptual approach grounded in policy and literature analysis, the study advances five propositions mapping Act 872 against the five Maqasid domains across the three pandemic phases. This article argues that integrating Maqasid al-Shariah into Malaysia's GIG economy governance offers a principled, human- centred, and values-driven framework for meaningful, human-centred reform has never been more urgent.

Transformasi ekonomi digital meningkatkan volume, kecepatan, dan kompleksitas informasi yang harus diproses organisasi dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Perkembangan artificial intelligence (AI) kemudian menggeser fungsi teknologi dari sekadar pendukung keputusan menuju penguatan kapasitas kognitif, kolaborasi manusia–AI, dan keterlibatan yang lebih luas dalam proses keputusan. Penelitian ini bertujuan mensintesis perkembangan peran AI dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis dan mengidentifikasi bagaimana perubahan tersebut membentuk arsitektur pengambilan keputusan baru dalam ekonomi digital. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif melalui qualitative thematic literature review. Penelusuran literatur dilakukan melalui basis data Scopus dan menghasilkan 1.326 rekaman awal, kemudian 1.303 rekaman unik. Setelah penyaringan akses full-text dan relevansi substantif, diperoleh 45 artikel untuk pemeriksaan penuh, dengan 38 artikel ditetapkan sebagai corpus inti. Analisis tematik menghasilkan empat tema utama: (1) pergeseran dari AI decision support menuju AI augmentation; (2) kolaborasi manusia–AI dan rekonstruksi pertimbangan manajerial; (3) perluasan peran generative AI dalam proses pengambilan keputusan; dan (4) trust, governance, serta batas kewenangan keputusan AI. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa transformasi AI tidak semata-mata mengarah pada penggantian manusia, tetapi pada reorganisasi pembagian kerja kognitif dan kewenangan keputusan antara manusia dan mesin. Berdasarkan temuan tersebut, penelitian mengusulkan konsep AI-Augmented Business Decision Architecture sebagai kerangka untuk memahami transformasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis di era ekonomi digital.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming children's digital environments, reshaping how they learn, interact, and participate as consumers. While existing scholarship and regulation largely emphasize digital safety—focusing on privacy protection and risk mitigation—there is limited attention to how AI can actively promote children's developmental well-being. This case study–based chapter advances a shift from digital safety to digital flourishing by examining how child-centered AI systems can support cognitive growth, social-emotional development, and ethical agency. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature and empirical case analyses of socially assistive robots, adaptive learning platforms, and conversational AI systems, the chapter develops a Developmental Flourishing Framework integrating developmental psychology, children's rights principles, and ethical marketing considerations. The analysis highlights both opportunities and structural risks, including algorithmic bias, surveillance practices, and persuasive design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores the use of digital political marketing strategies by Moroccan political parties, with a particular focus on voter engagement and the role of artificial intelligence (AI). Adopting a qualitative approach, the research is based on semi-structured interviews conducted with 16 participants, including political actors and external observers. Data were analyzed using a thematic analysis approach. The findings reveal that political parties primarily rely on social media and multi-channel communication strategies to engage voters, although these practices remain unevenly developed and largely conventional. While artificial intelligence is increasingly discussed as a transformative tool in political campaigns, its actual adoption in the Moroccan context remains limited, due to structural, organizational, and resource-related constraints. This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical insights into digital political marketing in an underexplored context and highlights the gap between theoretical advancements in AI and its practical implementation in political campaigns.

National geospatial infrastructures increasingly connect Earth Observation (EO), geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), interoperable services, and public-sector decision processes. However, an explicit method for assessing whether these technical functions operationalize the nine pathways of the United Nations Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (UN-IGIF) remains underdeveloped. This Communication develops a pathway-to-function-to-evidence assessment framework and applies it illustratively to the Rwanda Space Agency (RSA) GeoHub case. Using the UN-IGIF pathway definitions as normative criteria and the available GeoHub description as case material, we classify reported functions, map their institutional and technical dependencies, and identify the records required to substantiate operational performance and decision uptake. Worked mappings cover EO data stewardship, GeoAI processing, interoperable delivery, and sectoral decision workflows. The contribution is a transparent analytical procedure that distinguishes reported capabilities, proposed applications, and independently verified outcomes; it does not constitute an audit or quantitative impact evaluation. The framework offers a transferable basis for planning and evaluating EO-enabled geospatial infrastructures in emerging space ecosystems.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Finding training data in million-scale machine learning repositories is a Web search problem where text relevance is not enough. A query couples a semantic training goal with constraints such as task, license, and training stage, and the metadata that would verify them are often missing. Text retrieval ranks dataset cards by similarity but cannot enforce hard constraints or follow the relations that reach a sparsely described dataset. Free-form tool-calling agents are more flexible, but the same model that picks a dataset also declares it a match, and nothing checks that the query's constraints are actually met. Neither approach establishes that the data it returns will improve model training. To address it, we propose AgenticDS, a contract-governed agentic framework in which every language model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it. The framework compiles a query into a typed search plan, executes it through admissible deterministic operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and verifies the provenance-grounded evidence before accepting a ranking or emitting a typed diagnosis that permits only local repairs. On HuDS-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, AgenticDS improves NDCG@10 by 25.7\% over the strongest dense--sparse hybrid and by 18.9\% over a commercial LLM agent. A controlled search-to-train study further shows that the datasets it retrieves give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code, and medicine. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/nju-websoft/AgenticDS.

As autonomous artificial intelligence architectures transition from passive linguistic comprehension to active world simulation and real-world execution, the locus of economic power is shifting from static data storage to real-time operational data telemetry. While general-purpose AI models rely on post-hoc text archives and delayed historical records, global capital markets generate the densest, highest-frequency stream of human and algorithmic intent on Earth. However, legacy financial interfaces remain constrained by discrete, static text representations that force operators to process high-speed volatility through a severe cognitive and physiological bottleneck.The fundamental limitation is not merely the latency of information delivery, but the gap between receiving discrete observations of reality and perceiving the continuous evolution of the underlying system. DeltaSync addresses this gap by transforming real-time market telemetry into a motion-based representation of evolving market states, advancing the thesis that the next frontier of competitive advantage lies in the infrastructure through which reality becomes perceptible and actionable. This research paper introduces market motion and the DeltaSync Framework, a real-time perceptual architecture that converts discrete order book data into continuous optical flow fields. By offloading high-frequency market transitions from the slow parvocellular pathway (~70–100 ms) to the evolutionarily faster magnocellular pathway (~30–50 ms), the system achieves a measurable 20–50 ms cognitive lead time while maintaining mathematical losslessness (0.00% information loss). We establish that ownership of real-world perception infrastructure supersedes static data monopolies, paving the way for execution-based finance—a paradigm that replaces probabilistic, lagging risk-adjusted returns with deterministic cashflow precision. Keywords: M Magnocellular Pathway; Order Book Telemetry; Execution-Based Finance; Cognitive Latency; Optical Flow; Real-Time Perception; Algorithmic Trading Interfaces

AI in education is changing faster than conventional academic publishing can follow. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. Over a single evening in October 2026, a practitioner-scholar and an AI agent turned a body of 81 long-form newsletter articles on AI in education into ten thematic papers, each with original figures, verified references and an open disclosure of how it was made, and published them in Future Science Archives, a non-profit, open-review archive. The article sets out the motivation for the experiment, including the author's long interest in educational innovation and his concerns about the economics of academ‐ ic publishing. It describes the venue and its strengths and limitations, the source corpus, the workflow and the division of labour between human and AI, and the verification process, which found and corrected more than two dozen errors, unverifiable claims and one retracted study carried over from the newsletters. It reports the actual publication timeline. It then discusses the risks of the approach, including "research slop", weakened rigour and researchers becoming editors of machine-written text, and argues that these risks are real but manageable when the human remains responsible for judgement and the process is transparent. It closes with a replicable workflow for others.

Traditional assessment practices often do not align with active learning philosophies and, even where they do, are often subject to artificial intelligence use. Active learning offers an olive branch to these concerns, enabling students a way of demonstrating deeper understanding in a creative format. However, it also challenges us to consider how to reward the process, as well as the end product, and how to frame the participation involved accurately. This chapter introduces peer evaluation as a potential method for assessing team performance, and explains how this can be used to design a holistic model of student learning. Suggestions for successful implementation are given.

Medical education is evolving rapidly alongside the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs). Continuing medical education (CME) has traditionally relied on educational modalities sometimes conceptualized as the “three P’s” of Posters, Podium presentations, and Publications, later expanded into the “seven P’s” with the addition of Podcasts, Play, Peer-to-peer learning, and Patient interactions. This commentary proposes Prompting as an eighth “P” of CME, reflecting the growing importance of effectively interacting with AI systems in clinical and academic practice. Prompting refers to the process of crafting and refining instructions that guide AI-generated outputs. The quality, specificity, and contextual framing of prompts substantially influence the accuracy and usefulness of responses generated by LLMs. Emerging evidence suggests that prompting is a learnable skill that can improve educational and clinical utility without requiring advanced technical expertise. This commentary reviews key prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, role-based, chain-of-thought, and iterative prompting, and discusses their relevance to healthcare providers. Applications across clinical care, medical education, patient communication, administration, and research are explored. Potential benefits include generating differential diagnoses, summarizing medical literature, creating educational materials, supporting clinical simulations, and improving patient-facing communication. The commentary also addresses important risks associated with LLM use, including hallucinations, automation bias, and overreliance on AI-generated content. Ultimately, prompting is framed not only as a mechanism for learning through AI systems, but also as a modern medical literacy competency that healthcare providers must actively develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence has learned to predict electromagnetic responses rapidly and generate high-performance metasurface designs. However, one question remains open: compared with conventional design workflows that contain no learned model, has it made the complete design workflow faster, and are the resulting devices better? We argue that the answer depends on the task. Reading 100 highly cited optical studies in depth, we distinguish the design tasks in which artificial intelligence is irreplaceable, clearly advantageous, or without clear advantage. In our view, the key to the next decade is not more successes in isolated tasks but making each success a foundation for the field, through shifts such as shared data, trained models, and physics written into learning. Whether artificial intelligence leaves lasting value in this field will depend on whether its benefits can be verified, its methods transferred, and its designs corrected by experiment.

This scoping review mapped artificial intelligence (AI) applications in pediatric dentistry and evidence supporting clinical use. Searches covering 2022–2026 combined 957 records from six databases, 109 from a focused corrective search and 22 supplementary reports. Screening and record reconciliation yielded 179 included reports. Eight evaluation characteristics were mapped using six reporting states, with descriptive performance comparisons and exploratory sensitivity analyses. The largest domains were tooth detection, numbering and segmentation (38; 21.2%), risk, biomarkers and prevention (34; 19.0%), and caries imaging and developmental/age assessment (26 each; 14.5%). Ten reports (5.6%) documented external testing of varying independence and pediatric applicability; 22 included human or traditional-method comparators. Three evaluated clinician–AI assistance: two in technical segmentation and one in diagnosis. Ten examined workflow or use, three probability evaluation, eighteen subgroup performance or fairness, and seven patient-related outcomes. Main-article evidence was available for 153 reports; 26 relied on abstracts or excerpts. The main translational gap is evidence connecting technical performance to improved pediatric care. Priorities are prospective evaluation of diagnostic decisions and correction workload, independent calibration of risk models, and sustained patient outcomes. Revision-stage search restrictions and uneven source access limit generalization beyond the mapped evidence.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping how organizations monitor performance, translate strategic objectives into operational outcomes, and support managerial decision-making. This study examines digital performance management from an Information Systems perspective, focusing on the relationship between transformational leadership, strategic alignment, digital technologies, data-driven decision-making, and organizational performance. Building on an integrative review of the literature, the paper extends the traditional understanding of performance management by examining the growing role of information systems, digital dashboards, business intelligence, data analytics, and artificial intelligence in enabling continuous and increasingly real-time performance monitoring. The analysis suggests that transformational leadership provides an important organizational foundation for aligning people and strategic objectives, while digital performance management systems provide the informational infrastructure through which such alignment can be monitored, evaluated, and translated into managerial action. Based on this synthesis, the study proposes a conceptual framework connecting transformational leadership and strategic alignment with digital performance management systems, data-driven decision-making, and organizational performance. The framework highlights that technology alone is insufficient to improve performance and that its organizational value depends on leadership, appropriate performance indicators, information quality, digital capabilities, and a culture supportive of learning and continuous improvement. The study contributes to Information Systems research by integrating leadership and performance management perspectives with the digital infrastructures increasingly used to support organizational decision-making and performance improvement.

In the modern digital world, the growth of artificial intelligence and machine learning is changing the way we process and comprehend complex data. This chapter explains the principles and methods that enable machines to integrate and analyze data of multiple data types such as text, images, audio, and video. It brings in multimodal intelligence that is not the same as single modal approaches and also addresses the difficulty of non-homogeneous data combination. There are basic algorithms which are supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, and these have been discussed with multimodal representation, attention-based fusion, and cross-modal alignment. Its practical considerations such as scalability, robustness, interpretability, and mitigation of bias are also discussed in the chapter concerning real-world deployment. Finally, the gaps between the foundational ideas and the algorithmic approaches provide the reader with fundamental knowledge needed to create smart systems that can synthesize, reason, and make decisions based on various types of data to build a stronger foundation of AIs that can decide based on context.

Abstract The widespread adoption of video conferencing (VC) platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic has transformed synchronous higher education, yet sustaining student engagement in such environments remains a persistent challenge, particularly in creative disciplines. This study investigated the effectiveness of three gamification elements included animated badges, experience points, and level upgrades in enhancing behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement within a synchronous VC learning context. Guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study employed a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group design involving 124 first-year undergraduate graphic design students from three public universities in China. Participants were assigned to a non-gamified control group or one of three gamified conditions and completed pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring multidimensional engagement. Paired t-test analyses revealed statistically significant improvements across all engagement dimensions in the gamified groups (p < 0.001), while the control group exhibited minimal or no meaningful change. Experience points produced the most consistent gains across behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement, whereas level upgrades yielded the strongest effects on deep cognitive processing and metacognitive regulation. Animated badges were particularly effective in enhancing emotional engagement and learning enjoyment. One-way ANOVA results further indicated clear performance differentiation between gamified and non-gamified conditions. These findings displayed that well-designed gamification mechanisms can substantially enhance engagement in synchronous VC environments by supporting learners’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The study contributes empirical evidence to gamification and online learning literature and offers practical guidance for educators and platform designers seeking to improve motivation, interaction, and learning quality in real-time digital instruction.

Ethical principles are essential to the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare. This study examines the explicit lexical representation of predefined ethical themes in a selected corpus of 73 healthcare-AI publications. A nine-theme ethical codebook was developed from institutional guidance and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The study applied NLP-supported full-text analysis, inductive topic modeling, deductive codebook-guided content analysis, theme-based corpus analysis, and paper-level statistical comparison. The findings showed substantial variation in thematic representation. Fairness, accountability, and privacy received the strongest overall representation. Fairness had the highest raw keyword frequency, whereas accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate. Transparency showed moderate representation and was mainly associated with explainability-related discussion. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact showed the weakest representation, while safety, innovation and progress, and collaboration and partnership received comparatively less attention. Friedman and Holm-adjusted pairwise analyses confirmed significant differences among themes. These findings characterize patterns of ethical-theme representation within the selected healthcare-AI literature corpus. The study proposes measurable indicators to support future healthcare-AI research, governance, and responsible system development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
