documents.abstract: The modern approach to product creation is based not on intuitive ideas, but on the real-time analysis of users' digital behavior. It allows for predicting audience demands and actively shaping them by adapting the product to specific scenarios. Amid information overload, consumers place high demands on the quality and personalization of service. To build long-term relationships with the audience, brands need to ensure a seamless digital experience at all stages of interaction. The article explores modern innovative approaches to product development and promotion within the context of the economy's digital transformation. Special attention is paid to how digitalization is changing the logic of product creation and marketing communications: the focus shifts toward data, the speed of response to market demands, and the delivery of a seamless customer experience. The transformation of the product lifecycle stages is analyzed separately, covering the acceleration of time-to-market for new products through digital prototyping and split testing, dynamic positioning management based on real-time analytics, and the adaptation of promotion strategies to audience behavior on social media and marketplaces. The key tools shaping these new practices are examined, including artificial intelligence and machine learning for demand forecasting and offer adaptation, big data for segmentation and hypothesis testing, immersive technologies for audience engagement, and omnichannel systems. The research results allow for systemizing current innovative methods and offering practical recommendations for their implementation in organizations' marketing activities, taking into account the business's level of digital maturity and the specifics of the target audience. The recommendations on innovative approaches have been tested at an Omsk confectionery enterprise. The article will be of interest to corporate executives, marketers, and brand managers.

ABSTRACT: Conventional thermal processing methods such as drying, salting, fermentation, pasteurization, and sterilization remain the backbone of food processing and preservation. However, heat-induced losses of vitamins, pigments, bioactive compounds, and texture quality often compel manufacturers to explore alternative approaches to satisfy evolving consumer demands. In response to the increasing preference for minimally processed foods that retain nutritional quality and fresh-like characteristics, researchers and industry stakeholders have turned to innovative non-thermal and advanced processing technologies. This comprehensive review evaluates the current landscape of non-thermal technologies, including high hydrostatic pressure (HHP), pulsed electric field (PEF), ultrasonication (US), cold plasma (CP), UV irradiation (UVC), and ozonation, that effectively inactivate spoilage and pathogenic microorganisms while operating at ambient or modest temperatures. Additionally, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) optimization for these technologies are explored, highlighting their potential to enhance process efficiency, predict microbial inactivation kinetics, and optimize nutritional retention. These methods preserve sensory qualities, improve techno-functional properties, support better digestibility and oxidative stability, and significantly extend shelf life across various food matrices with minimal thermal degradation. Keywords: Food processing, non-thermal technologies, hydrostatic pressure, ultrasonication, ozonation, oxidative stability, machine learning, artificial intelligence, process optimization

RÉSUMÉIntroduction. L'intelligence artificielle (IA) constitue une innovation majeure susceptible de transformer les pratiques dentaires, mais son intégration dans les pays en développement soulève des questions spécifiques. Cette étude avait pour but d'explorer les inquiétudes et les attentes des chirurgiens-dentistes ivoiriens concernant l'intégration de l'IA en odontologie. Méthodologie. Étude descriptive et transversale menée de janvier à mai 2025 à Abidjan, auprès de 68 chirurgiens-dentistes en exercice, volontaires et consentants. Les étudiants en formation initiale et les praticiens retraités ont été exclus. L'échantillonnage était stratifié proportionnel selon le type de structure d'exercice (public et privé), avec une sélection aléatoire simple au sein de chaque strate. Les données ont été recueillies par un questionnaire standardisé auto-administré, pré-testé auprès de 15 praticiens, structuré en cinq sections : données sociodémographiques, connaissances sur l'IA, perceptions générales, attentes et perspectives, et dispositions à adopter l'IA. Les données ont été saisies et analysées avec IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. Résultats. L'âge moyen des praticiens était de moins de 30 ans dans 41 % des cas, et 53 % avaient moins de 5 ans d'expérience. La grande majorité (96 %) avait déjà entendu parler de l'IA appliquée à l'odontologie, mais 84 % n'avaient jamais utilisé d'outils d'IA dans leur pratique. L'imagerie radiographique constituait le domaine le plus influencé (88 %). La majorité (94 %) considérait que l'IA pourrait améliorer la pratique odontologique. Les principales inquiétudes étaient la déshumanisation de la relation patient-praticien (62 %) et le coût élevé des équipements (59 %). Tous les participants se déclaraient favorables à une formation en IA, privilégiant les ateliers pratiques en présentiel (50–55 %). Conclusion. L'IA représente une opportunité importante pour le développement de l'odontologie en Côte d'Ivoire. Son intégration effective nécessite une meilleure formation des praticiens, une accessibilité accrue aux technologies et un encadrement éthique et réglementaire adapté.ABSTRACTIntroduction. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a major innovation likely to transform dental practices, but its integration in developing countries raises specific questions. This study had as its purpose to explore the concerns and expectations of Ivorian dentists regarding the integration of AI in dentistry. Methods. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from January to May 2025 in Abidjan, among 68 practising dentists who were volunteers and consented. Students in initial training and retired practitioners were excluded. Proportional stratified sampling by type of practice (public and private) was used, with simple random selection within each stratum. Data were collected using a standardized self-administered questionnaire, pre-tested with 15 practitioners, structured in five sections: sociodemographic data, knowledge about AI, general perceptions, expectations and perspectives, and willingness to adopt AI. Data were entered and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. Results. The age group under 30 years was the most represented (41%), and 53% had less than 5 years of experience. The vast majority (96%) had heard of AI applied to dentistry, but 84% had never used AI-based tools in their practice. Radiographic imaging was the area most influenced (88%). Most practitioners (94%) believed that AI could improve dental practice. The main concerns were dehumanization of the patient-practitioner relationship (62%) and the high cost of equipment (59%). All participants were in favour of AI training, preferring practical in-person workshops (50–55%). Conclusion. AI represents a significant opportunity for the development of dentistry in Côte d'Ivoire. Its effective integration requires better training for practitioners, increased access to technology, and appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.

documents.abstract: This study presents an extension of an industrial augmented reality (AR) and artificial intelligence (AI) disassembly station with inspection functions for reusable components recovered from end-of-life washing machines. While prior work focused on monitor-based AR guidance and AI-supported validation of disassembly steps, this paper addresses the next integration step: inspection-aware AR workflows that connect worker guidance, AI/sensor-based condition assessment, human confirmation, and reuse documentation. Specifically, we outline how inspection procedures for the two most valuable components targeted for reuse (printed circuit boards (PCBs) and the washing unit) can be integrated into the station concept. For PCBs, a burn-damage classification pipeline was developed. Preliminary frame-level validation on an independent real-world dataset showed that several models detect most visibly burnt PCB views, but their low specificity currently prevents autonomous reuse decisions. The AI component is therefore used as a preliminary screening and warning mechanism whose output is reviewed by the worker. For the washing unit, the developed testing device demonstrates the feasibility of pressure-loss and vibration measurements directly after disassembly; these measurements are presently proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than quantitatively validated diagnostics. The primary contribution of this Brief Research Report is therefore the system-level integration of AR guidance, visual and sensor-based assessment, human confirmation, reuse classification, and documentation into one continuous worker-facing workflow. The results establish integrated feasibility and preliminary validation rather than industrial inspection reliability.

Background/Objectives: Adolescence is a critical developmental period for establishing health behaviors that shape long-term well-being and chronic disease risk. However, many adolescents do not meet recommendations for physical activity (PA), diet, screen time, or sleep. This review examines the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents’ health behaviors. It synthesizes the existing literature on the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents’ health behaviors, with a focus on four areas: design, feasibility, impact, safety and ethics. Methods: This narrative review synthesized adolescent-focused studies and relevant studies involving children, young adults, mixed-age samples, or unspecified populations when their findings were applicable to adolescent health behavior interventions. The evidence was organized around chatbot design, feasibility, behavioral outcomes, and safety and ethical issues. Results: Selected studies reported favorable usability, satisfaction, or engagement during brief evaluations. Adaptive personalization, contextual prompting, and theory-guided dialogue were reported design features, but their contributions to sustained engagement or behavioral outcomes remain uncertain. However, evidence of behavioral impact of AI chatbots remains limited and uneven across behavior domains (i.e., PA, dietary intake, screen time, and sleep). Safety and ethical concerns include accuracy and misinformation, privacy and data governance, and clear escalation and safety protocols. Conclusions: AI chatbots warrant further investigation for adolescent health behavior promotion. Current evidence does not establish general acceptability, sustained engagement, or behavior change efficacy, and further research should evaluate these outcomes alongside safety and ethical safeguards.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and reference management technologies is transforming academic writing practices in higher education. This qualitative instrumental case study investigates how generative AI and reference management tools are integrated into assignment writing at Zimbabwe Open University within an Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) environment. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with seven lecturers and one quality assurance coordinator, as well as focus group discussions with fourteen students selected through purposive sampling. Guided by the Constructivist Learning Theory, the study examined the pedagogical implications of AI-supported writing practices. Findings reveal that tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly and Mendeley enhance writing quality, research efficiency, accessibility, and learner confidence. However, concerns regarding overreliance, academic integrity and diminished critical engagement were also identified. The study recommends the development of institutional policies, ethical training frameworks and curriculum adjustments to promote responsible and pedagogically sound integration of generative AI tools in ODeL contexts.

Security Operation Centres (SOCs) must validate large volumes of alerts with limited analyst resources, yet alerts often lack sufficient context to determine whether suspicious activity is attack related. While provenance-based intrusion detection research has progressed from perception-level signals to comprehension- and projection-level cyber situational awareness (CSA), it remains unclear whether richer CSA consistently improves alert validation. This paper presents the first systematic evaluation of perception-, comprehension-,and projection-level CSA within a unified alert validation framework. Using Captain and Kairos, we generate multi-level CSA and formulate alert validation as a positive-unlabelled multi-instance learning (PU-MIL) task over CSA-derived behavioural hypotheses. Experimental evaluation on the DARPA TC dataset shows that comprehension-level CSA substantially improves validation by incorporating causal attack context. Relative to the Queue and Max. CSG baselines, PU-MIL achieves up to 28.6 and 75 percentage-point gains in Recall@5, and 24.6% and 86.8% reductions in mean positive rank on Cadets and Theia, respectively. Projection-level CSA can yield additional benefits, reducing the mean positive rank on Theia from 22.0 to 8.5 at a 40-minute projection horizon, although its effectiveness varies across projection horizons. Overall, richer CSA does not necessarily lead to better alert validation. Rather, its value depends on when and how it is introduced, motivating adaptive CSA progression that selectively enriches alerts according to validation requirements.

Objective: This review critically examined artificial intelligence (AI) applications in canine echocardiography, automated measurement and disease classification strategies, validation designs, and the requirements for safe clinical translation. Method: A narrative review was conducted. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 20 October 2026, supplemented by screening the reference lists of identified articles, and studies that applied machine learning or deep learning to canine echocardiograms were selected by relevance. Results: In the clinical veterinary setting, two studies addressed automated ventricular measurements through anatomical landmark localization and staging of myxomatous mitral valve disease through echocardiography–radiography fusion. An additional group of experimental studies applied deep learning to left ventricular segmentation and motion tracking in dogs. The main challenges identified were operator variability, breed-related anatomical heterogeneity, the lack of multicenter validation, and reliance on imperfect reference standards. Conclusions: The clinical usefulness of these models requires patient- and center-level evaluation, uncertainty quantification, agreement studies against specialists, and analysis of errors near treatment thresholds. A two-stage research pathway, measurement followed by classification, was proposed, complemented by prospective assessment and veterinary oversight.

documents.abstract: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.

The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education programming raises questions about its influence on learning autonomy and critical thinking. This stems from theoretical concerns about technological dependency and from the limited regional empirical evidence on how these effects vary by experience level. This quantitative study examines whether experience level (novices vs. advanced) and AI usage frequency associate with these constructs among computer science students in Costa Rica. Using a cross-sectional design, 99 students from Universidad Hispanoamericana de Costa Rica were classified as novices (n = 79) or advanced (n = 20), via the Dreyfus & Dreyfus (1986) model with 5 weighted indicators. Accordingly, autonomy (а = 0,685) and critical thinking (а = 0,742) were measured, and both constructs were analyzed using Welch t-tests, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression. Autonomy showed suggestive evidence of being higher in advanced students [t(49,2) = 2,079, p = 0,043, g = 0,386], though nonparametric analysis did not confirm this [U = 614,5, p = 0,125]. Critical thinking showed no significant difference [t(42,1) = 1,816, p = 0,077, g = 0,361], and AI usage frequency was not associated with autonomy [r = 0,166, p = 0,101] or critical thinking [r = 0,123, p = 0,226]. Both constructs showed robust correlation [r = 0,552, p < 0,001; р = 0,533, p < 0,001]. The 88,9 % active modification rate suggests students use AI as cognitive support, potentially explaining the null associations. Given that 85,9 % support regulated use and 10,1 % favor prohibition, these preliminary findings suggest that promoting ethical regulated AI use may be preferable to restriction.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education by enabling intelligent assistive technologies that enhance learning outcomes for students with disabilities. This chapter examines the landscape of AI-driven assistive tools—including speech recognition, adaptive learning platforms, natural language processing, and predictive analytics—and their role in advancing inclusive education. Drawing on recent systematic reviews and empirical studies, it critically evaluates opportunities such as personalized accommodation, improved accessibility, and universal design for learning (UDL) integration, alongside challenges including algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital equity. Frameworks for ethical AI deployment and institutional policy recommendations are presented. The chapter concludes with future directions for sustainable, human-centered AI assistive ecosystems in higher education.

Financial forecasting is a core aspect of contemporary financial systems, and it helps to support some of the most important activities of a financial system, including investment planning, portfolio optimization, and risk management. The traditional forecasting models, which are mainly statistical and econometric models, are often based on assumptions of linearity and limited datasets and therefore have limited capability to accurately model the complex, volatile and nonlinear behaviour of financial markets. This paper will give a detailed comparison and contrast of the different AI and ML methods used in financial forecasting, such support vectors machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, reinforcement learning (RL) and natural language processing (NLP). Overall, this paper demonstrates that AI and ML can have a transformative potential in the context of financial forecasting because it has the potential to develop more intelligent, responsive and efficient financial decision-making systems.

Background: Accurate diagnostic image interpretation is fundamental to safe radiological practice, yet training opportunities vary in case exposure and access to expert feedback. Intelligent and adaptive tutoring systems offer a potential means of providing more individualised learning. Such systems have been developed in radiology over several decades, ranging from early computer-based tutors to contemporary AI-enabled platforms. Existing reviews of artificial intelligence in radiology education have focused largely on educational applications, curricula and outcomes, rather than systematically examining the development of tutoring systems for diagnostic image interpretation. Aim: To map the design, development, implementation and evaluation of intelligent and adaptive tutoring systems for diagnostic image interpretation in radiology education. Methods: A scoping review will be conducted using JBI methodology and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, IEEE Xplore and Scopus were searched, supplemented by citation searching. Eligible reports describe computer-based systems that teach or assess diagnostic image interpretation and incorporate an intelligent, adaptive or learner-responsive tutoring component. Data will be charted at system level across key technical, educational and evaluation characteristics and synthesized descriptively. Expected outcomes: The review will characterize the development and evaluation of intelligent tutoring approaches in radiology, describe the range of system designs used, and identify gaps and priorities for future research.

documents.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets tabular foundation models make predictions without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. These models achieve strong predictive accuracy, but interpreting how individual features contribute to the prediction remains difficult. In biology, for example, feature contributions can help identify biomarkers or risk genes. Post-hoc interpretability methods assign feature importance scores, but these scores do not indicate what the model actually uses and can lead to explanation errors. We introduce TICL$^3$ (Tabular In-Context Local Linear Learning), an interpretable-by-design predictor that uses a tabular foundation model to guide a simple linear prediction rule. TICL$^3$ first learns a shared linear model to capture dataset-level feature effects. Then, for each query, it retrieves similar training samples using representations from the foundation model and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood. The shared model captures broad effects, while the local model corrects errors among similar samples. Their combined coefficients determine each feature contribution to the final query-specific linear score, so the same model makes and explains the prediction. Across 386 classification benchmark-dataset evaluations, TICL$^3$ trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and outperforms CatBoost in 266 evaluations. It improves average support F1 over MAPLE by 4.7 points and achieves the best performance on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has disrupted established assessment practices in higher education, producing widespread uncertainty about what counts as appropriate student work and how it should be evaluated. The introductory chapter argues that this uncertainty is not simply a temporary lack of clarity but reflects a deeper challenge in how assessment distinguishes between student achievement and the tools students use. Drawing on the idea of wicked problems, it suggests that this challenge cannot be definitively resolved, but must instead be worked through in context by focusing on how boundaries in assessment are being drawn, interpreted, and contested under AI conditions. This introduction uses this framing to orient the chapters that follow, showing how they contribute to understanding and respond to these changes from different perspectives. The volume that follows then brings together conceptual, empirical, and forward-looking work to examine how assessment is evolving, why these changes matter, and how educators might respond. Rather than offering a single model of AI-ready assessment, it provides a set of resources for understanding the problem and navigating it in practice.

This introduction sets out the problem the book addresses: the absence of a comprehensive framework under African human rights law governing the use of artificial intelligence by social media platforms. It situates that problem within the rapid global adoption of artificial intelligence across public and private sectors, the proliferation of national and regional strategies and ethical principles, and the African vision on the regulation of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. It explains why social media platforms occupy a central place in this debate, given business models built on retention and the suitability of artificial intelligence for inference, personalisation, and targeting at scale. The introduction then sets out the book’s structure, explaining the selection of three rights most affected by these technologies, and the rationale for treating each according to the developmental stage of the right within African jurisprudence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence is pushing beyond unimodal paradigms, paving the way for sophisticated multimodal systems that can process and relate information from diverse sources such as text, images, audio, and sensor data. This chapter serves as a foundational introduction to AI-driven multimodal intelligence, outlining the core principles, architectures, and transformative potential of these systems. We begin by defining key concepts, contrasting multimodal learning with traditional unimodal approaches, and highlighting the inherent challenges of data heterogeneity, alignment, and fusion. The chapter then delves into the primary technical architectures for multimodal integration, including early, late, and hybrid fusion strategies, with a focus on modern neural approaches like cross-modal attention and transformers. Beyond the algorithms, we discuss the critical pipeline from data processing and feature extraction to model training and cross-modal reasoning. Finally, the chapter sets the stage for the rest of the book by underscoring the real-world implications of this technology, from enhancing accessibility to revolutionizing human–computer interaction, while also acknowledging the ongoing research challenges in robustness, interpretability, and ethical deployment.

Despite the growing body of research involving examining teachers’ and students’ experiences of AI integration in EFL writing pedagogy in Bangladesh, relatively little is known about English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s influence in major domains of EFL writing. To bridge this gap, our research investigates tertiary-level English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact in developing their EFL writing skills within the Bangladeshi context through employing a mixed-method research design, comprising both quantitative and qualitative data. Quantitative data were collected from 74 undergraduate and graduate students at a public university in Bangladesh using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and subsequently, qualitative insights were gathered to supplement the survey data through three focus group discussions (FGDs). Our study explored ChatGPT’s perceived role across four key domains of EFL writing: motivation and engagement, grammatical correction, writing essays and creating references. Findings revealed that ChatGPT positively influenced students’ motivation through providing immediate and non-judgmental feedback, facilitating idea generation, content organization and context-specific writing. Also, ChatGPT facilitated the pre-writing and foundational stages of essay writing. Students exhibited more caution regarding ChatGPT’s role as a grammar correction and referencing tool. Despite its usefulness in explaining grammar rules and providing language-related feedback, students found specialized grammar correction tools to be more reliable than ChatGPT. Likewise, ChatGPT emerged as an unreliable referencing tool due to producing misleading citation information. Our study offers key implications for educators, stakeholders and policy- makers to integrate ChatGPT more ethically and effectively in EFL writing while preserving independent reasoning and judicious evaluation. Spectrum, Volume 19, June 2024: 135-149

Collaborative augmented reality (AR) systems are increasingly used for technical training, yet limited evidence exists on how instructional design choices affect learning and transfer. This study examined the effects of onboarding strategy and task demonstration modality in a multiuser AR environment for motor control unit setup and lockout-tagout training. Eighty participants were assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects study: checklist versus interactive onboarding and video versus avatar-based demonstration. Participants completed AR-based training and then performed the procedure on physical equipment. Results showed that avatar-based demonstrations produced significantly greater learning gains, while video-based demonstrations produced fewer procedural errors during physical transfer. Onboarding strategy did not significantly affect objective learning or transfer outcomes. These findings reveal an important design tradeoff: immersive avatar demonstrations may strengthen conceptual understanding, whereas physically grounded video demonstrations may better support real-world procedural transfer. The study provides evidence-based guidance for designing collaborative AR training systems in technical workforce education.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Health guidance is a topic that has been gaining increasing traction in the past few years. Specifically, apps utilizing AI to provide health guidance and allow users to track macronutrient content have been gaining prevalence in recent research. However, current apps require users to manually input all information into the app. Therefore, this work seeks to evaluate the effectiveness of the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, a multimodal large language model (LLM), in analyzing the macronutrient content (i.e., proteins, fats, and carbohydrates) in food images. We tested 100 dishes randomly sampled from the Nutrition5k dataset. Each image was queried three times with three different prompt phrasings and the estimated values were compared with the ground truth values in the dataset. For the baseline prompt, the mean absolute error (MAE) was 4.1 g for protein, 3.6 g for fat, and 6.1 g for carbohydrates, and the median absolute percentage errors were 29.9%, 29.2%, and 32.1% respectively. The mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 38.5% for protein but 211.2% for fats and 442.7% for carbohydrates, which were inflated due to a small number of dishes containing less than 0.5 g of fat or carbohydrate, where errors of a few grams produced errors in the thousands. Without dishes with less than 2 g of the nutrient, the MAPE was 38.5%, 33.6%, and 33.5%. On metrics not sensitive to near-zero values, error was of similar size across the three macronutrients, and protein was underestimated on average, with the largest errors concentrated in a subset of dishes. MAE differed by at most 0.6 g across prompt wordings, although fat MdAPE was higher under both alternative prompts. Because no confidence intervals or significance tests were computed, these are observations from a single 100-dish sample rather than established differences. Additionally, the 100 dishes selected for the study came from a 400-dish subset whose selection cannot be reproduced.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

This chapter examines the principles and structures that underpin effective investigation management, and it emphasises that organised processes, robust governance, and strategic oversight enhance investigative success and safeguard justice. It outlines governance frameworks, clarifies the role of the (P)GSB, and establishes an Overarching Investigative Strategy that integrates major incident rooms, allocates appropriate resources, and defines enquiry team roles. The chapter defines aims, objectives, and terms of reference, and it explains how investigators prioritise lines of enquiry, manage information flow, and maintain clear and consistent communication across complex operations. It describes action management systems, situation reporting, and handover procedures, and it promotes organisational learning alongside the careful use of artificial intelligence to support efficiency and decision-making. Finally, the chapter addresses disclosure obligations and demonstrates that disciplined management, transparent processes, and continuous evaluation ensure accountability, reduce error, and maintain investigative integrity.

As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($κ$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: Current generative AI models solve introductory physics problems at expert level. Kortemeyer (2026) reports that GPT-5 Thinking scores 27/30 on physics finals and 92.3% on a representation translation test, categorizing problems by solution method rather than surface features: a hallmark of expert cognition. As of summer 2026, most standard kinematics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems can be solved almost instantaneously. Small accommodations accumulate quietly: allowing AI-generated visualizations here, AI-assisted explanations there. The real danger lies not in incorrect outputs, but in the gradual erosion of students' engagement in epistemic practices: the ways of thinking, predicting, and evaluating evidence that define scientific reasoning. Kortemeyer calls this the "boiling frog problem": educational systems may adapt so incrementally to AI capabilities that their foundational learning goals are no longer questioned until it is too late to reverse course. This paper proposes a constructive, classroom-ready answer at the level of individual instructional design. It presents AIRIS as a deliberately practice-oriented condensation of a broader, more fine-grained theoretical account of how cognitive regulation is distributed in hybrid human-AI cognition. Drawing on research in self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, AIRIS structures student work across three phases: before, during, and after AI use. The relevant question is not whether AI augments performance (it undeniably does), but whether that augmentation enhances or displaces the cognitive work essential to learning. The answer lies not in the tool, but in the task.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: To save cost, practitioners often ask a language model to grade many independent items in one prompt. This assumes that verdicts are separable: that the verdict on an item does not depend on the other items in the prompt or on its position among them. Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading and review star ratings) and five open-weight models with 4-9B parameters, assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming the item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading only by -0.033 to +0.010; for four models with 14-32B parameters, 6-15% of decisions change, 4.2-9.1 points more. We show that flip rates decompose exactly into components of order, slot and membership, and that under a threshold model they grow with the square root of the variance that the context contributes, so that effects that are small for scores are large for decisions. Most of the latent dissimilarity between partitions comes from the order of the neighbours and the slot. The main effect of which items share the prompt, the part that voting over permutations of a batch cannot remove, accounts for 0.11-0.22 of it, and majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of the flips. Batched verdicts also differ systematically from single-item verdicts: even the majority of fifteen random batches disagrees with them on 8.4-17.8% of decisions. Editing a single generation shows that both the model's own earlier verdicts and the neighbours' texts carry the effect. On the easy task, star ratings, only 2.9-3.9% of decisions change. We recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost with a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: For one to achieve meaningful learning, Knowledge acquisition is a very crucial factor that should never be undermined, however, we should also note that the learner's possession of information does not necessarily mean that he understands all the concepts or is able to apply them in unfamiliar situations. This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Lectures and other educators can provide all the necessary explanations and provide foundational knowledge, but they may not support mastery when they are used as the only instructional method or when majorly paired with recall-based examinations. Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. Cascaded passive RLC ladder networks Deterministic Reinforcement Learning Verifier:The package provides an exact, rule-based reward model (laplace_cot_verifier) offering zero-inference-cost reward modeling for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Large language models (LLMs) are emerging enablers of industrial information integration, yet their adoption mechanisms in construction remain unclear. This study develops an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model and the Information Systems Success model, extended with trust, prior LLM experience, perceived substitution crisis, and job specialization, to explain individual adoption of LLMs for information integration in construction. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 82 Chinese construction professionals are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Results show that perceived ease of use robustly strengthens attitude and provides directional evidence for strengthening perceived usefulness, while perceived usefulness strengthens attitude and attitude drives intention to use. Trust, reinforced by perceived information quality, shows a positive association with intention under the primary one-tailed criterion, but this relationship requires further validation under the two-tailed robustness check. System quality and information quality indirectly foster adoption by improving perceived ease of use, although the relationship between system quality and trust is supported only as directional evidence, while prior LLM experience enhances ease of use but not perceived usefulness or trust. Perceived substitution crisis and job specialization exhibit no significant effects. The findings highlight that successful LLM-enabled information integration depends on both technical quality and psychological appraisals, and they offer implications for designing trustworthy, humancentered LLM applications that advance intelligent, interconnected construction ecosystems. The study links micro-level user acceptance with macro-level digital transformation and integration strategic objectives.

This theoretical paper examines how educational leaders can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for equity-focused school and district improvement. Although prior improvement leadership research connects equity-focused leadership, improvement science, and workplace culture (Shepard, 2026), AI use in education remains largely focused on individual use, leaving less understood about what changes when GenAI becomes part of an improvement team. Drawing on equity-focused leadership, improvement science, workplace culture, and human-AI teaming, the paper introduces the Human-AI Team Improvement Framework. The framework centers equity-focused collaborative continuous improvement and identifies three interdependent leadership conditions (co-inquiry, empowered ownership, and courageous safety) that support humans and GenAI in working, learning, and improving together. The framework focuses attention on the leadership conditions needed for human-AI teams to work and learn together in improvement. It suggests that GenAI may help teams address immediate problems while also building their capacity to inquire, learn, and improve. The paper concludes with implications for educational leaders and directions for research on human-AI improvement teams in practice.

The purpose of this study is to explore the factors motivating immigrants to migrate to Sweden and the factors influencing immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden. To address this, the study include two inter-related research questions; (1) what factors influence the immigrants to migrate to Sweden? And (2) what are the leading motivational factors that influence immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden? This study grounded in the push and pull theory. The push and pull theory was used to understand both the research questions, which are motivations behind immigrants’ decision to migrate to Sweden and the motivations of immigrants to become entrepreneurs in Sweden. The study has followed purely the qualitative research method in accordance with abductive approach which allowed the author to move back and forth between data and theory. Data were collected through 11 semi-structured interviews of immigrants who became entrepreneurs in Sweden. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify common patterns in the data. The findings indicate that the immigrants are motivated to migrate to Sweden as a result of expecting future prospects, educational aspirations, environment and career related opportunities and family related concerns. Further the immigrants pursue their entrepreneurial journey as a result of motivational factors such as previous influences and experiences, intrinsic motivations and personal characteristics, support system influences, financial incentives, barriers in the labour market, perceived ease of entrepreneurship and business environment related factors.

Most school responses to generative AI begin with tools: which platform to license, which training day to run, which policy to publish. This article argues that the order is backwards. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on curriculum reform and institutional change, it examines AI in schools as a leadership problem. It sets out five pressures that leaders face: a speed gap between students' adoption of AI and institutions' capacity to govern it; a purpose question about what school is for when knowledge is freely available; an ecosystem problem, in which reforms fail not at the design stage but in the system of assessment, professional learning and routines they land in; a sequencing problem, in which institutions buy tools before doing the human work that makes them useful; and a structural shift in which families increasingly unbundle schooling. It proposes a five-step leadership sequence (purpose, conversation, red lines, ecosystem align‐ ment and iteration) and argues that leaders should separate two decisions that are usually treated as one: what AI should free time for, and how fast the institution should move.

Debate about generative AI in education often asks whether it is good or bad for learning. A 2026 expert consensus report from the University of Minnesota, UNC-Chapel Hill and UC Irvine argues that this question is too blunt. Thirty experts used a preregistered Delphi method to rate 65 learning processes for how likely general-purpose generative AI is to enhance or disrupt them, reaching consensus on 42. The pattern they describe can be read as a sequence: AI threatens the early work of taking in new information, can support the consolidation of what has been learned, and does not yet reliably support higher-order thinking and transfer. The report also rates the strength of the existing evidence as low. This review asks whether the experimental and observational studies published so far are consistent with that consensus. It maps a field experiment with high-school mathematics students, a randomised con‐ trolled trial of an AI physics tutor, an EEG study of essay writing, and survey research on cognitive offloading onto the three stages of the sequence. The studies largely agree with the experts. Unrestricted answer-giving harms acquisition. Tutor-style designs built on learning science can strengthen consolidation. Offloading thinking is linked with weaker critical thinking. We summarise this as a 'learn first, then use AI' principle, link it to established learning science, and set out implications for teachers, school leaders and researchers.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how learning designers (LDs) mediate and lead assessment transformation in higher education in response to the rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Drawing on cross-institutional interviews with 11 LDs from six Australian and New Zealand universities, it identifies ways that LDs are enacting their roles in response to GenAI: agents of change; emotional and cultural navigators; strategic influencers and policy shapers; designers of assessment; technical specialists and tool curators; and advocates for equity and inclusion. Situated within Whitchurch’s notion of the third space , LDs act as boundary spanners who translate institutional imperatives and academic values into coherent pedagogical practice. Their work supports transforming institutional ‘AI shock’ into opportunities for innovation, embedding authentic, reflective, and inclusive assessment practices. The chapter argues that LDs’ relational and strategic expertise is valuable in reimagining assessment for an AI-mediated educational future and calls for their recognition as co-leaders in shaping policy, pedagogy, and institutional culture.

This study examines how scientists in interdisciplinary programs learn from one another during collaboration. Researchers who participated in large scale research projects on human-AI teaming were surveyed about their collaborative experiences. Survey results show that regular cross-team meetings, careful listening, and adaptive communication are central to effective integration, while terminology conflicts and coordination costs persist. Findings highlight interaction structures and integrative roles as key levers for improving interdisciplinary teamwork. Framed within the context of the science of team science, the discussion highlights the support needed for interdisciplinary structures and processes enabling effective scientific collaboration.

Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Few-Shot Action Recognition (FSAR) widely use in Action Recognition domains with limited labeled data, such as medical surgery. Existing FSAR methods often rely on single-modal approaches, which suffer from limited feature representation and a lack of semantic understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoMA, a novel Mamba-based multimodal FSAR framework, designed to optimize the learning of multimodal information and improve the performance of few-shot action recognition tasks. MoMA integrates a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to generate semantically rich representations from both textual and video data, which are then aligned and fused with visual features. To address the challenges of domain-specific prior knowledge and intra-class variance, we introduce a dual-branch contrastive learning architecture that reinforces category distinctions and mitigates the accumulation of intra-class heterogeneity. Our experimental results show that MoMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the HMDB51, Kinetics, and SSv2 datasets, achieving improvements of 1.5%, 1.9%, and 3.5%, respectively, in the 1-shot setting.

Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

The rising pressure on lifestyle related illnesses including obesity, diabetes and heart diseases, has heightened pressure on the need to develop digital health solutions in an intelligent and scalable manner. The paper describes LiveFit, which is AI-enhanced customized nutrition and subscription-based health management software, which combines real-time monitoring of macronutrients, automatically adjusted diet, online ordering of meal plans, and an interface available across platforms. The suggested system adheres to a layered structure, which comprises a web-based dashboard, a Node.js-based microservice configuration and the MongoDB Atlas cloud storage, as well as a React Native (Expo Router) application. JWT-based authentication is used to ensure secure communication and brings scaling to data processing and user interactions which are facilitated by cloud-hosted APIs. The system will integrate the logic of contextual recommendation which dynamically examines nutritional intake and gives personal feedback in terms of perceived deficiencies. In contrast to other traditional calorie counting programs, LiveFit is aimed at active nutritional evaluation and dynamic intervention as opposed to passive dieting over a record. Experimental analysis proves the stable system operation, average API response time does not exceed 200 ms, and the accuracy of authentication is stable with as much as multi-user dependence. The suggested framework identifies the possibility to use artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, and subscription-based models to provide adaptive and scalable preventive healthcare systems.

Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution. This evaluation cost can delay design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development. We present a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions. We applied it to the human-supervised development of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on a Artix-7 FPGA. For the same CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation, including implementation, was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation. In one case, board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run. The result guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.

Personalized fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) enhances user experience but incurs substantial computational costs. Recent studies show that initializing training from a style-similar fine-tuned model reduces adaptation overhead, turning such checkpoints into reusable, tradable assets. A marketplace for these checkpoints, however, faces information asymmetry: sellers may misreport a checkpoint's style, while buyers cannot verify its usefulness before purchase, which invites adverse selection. We introduce LLM eBay, a simple single-round marketplace for trading fine-tuned LLMs. Sellers are paid per purchase at a posted price, and a truncated quadratic proper scoring rule adjusts each payment according to how well the seller's style report agrees with a style signal that the platform measures by generating text on hidden prompts. We show that the score elicits the verifier's expected signal, characterize exactly when truthful reporting is a seller best response under per-purchase demand, and bound the downside risk from noisy verification. In an end-to-end study with real LoRA checkpoints on two base models and three buyer tasks, LLM eBay reduces measured convergence steps by 8.5\% relative to retrieval over self-reported style (95\% CI [1.0\%, 15.9\%]). In model-based market simulations built on a measured style-to-cost relationship, it cuts style-claim error by 96.5\% (from 0.424 to 0.015), recovers 96.3\% of Oracle welfare, saves 72.4\% of the cost of fine-tuning from the base model, and keeps all providers profitable in the default setting.

Serverless execution of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming important, reflecting their wide societal use. An increasingly present stage in LLM pipelines is fine-tuning, which specializes trained models and improves inference performance. Serverless operation of LLM fine-tuning workloads shifts operational concerns from the user to the provider. For these new workloads, providers face important operational complexities, such as performance issues, resource waste, and even service failure due to misconfiguration. However, optimizing such workloads is still at an early stage, and, relevant to this work, relatively little is currently known about how LLM fine-tuning workloads run in practice. In this work, we address the knowledge gap by characterizing the execution of LLM fine-tuning workloads on clusters equipped with different GPUs, running LLM models at various scales. We analyze IBM's LLMFineTuningBench, a large-scale, diverse profiling dataset of 30,920 fine-tuning experiments that records both successful and failing configurations. We provide quantitative insight into throughput (expressed in tokens/s), scaling, failure, and potential for performance optimization for four commonly used GPU types, in setups of 1 to 32 GPUs. We find that (1) job feasibility (run or fail) depends on workload properties, with failure ratios rising from 52% for small batch sizes (16-64) up to 95% for the largest (1,024); (2) throughput grows logarithmically with batch size; (3) scaling is near-linear when the workload is deployed intra-node, and optimizations such as RoCE substantially improves efficiency for inter-node deployment (e.g., 0.72 vs. 0.26 efficiency without RoCE); and (4) system-level optimizations can outweigh application-level ones (RoCE, up to 2.9$\times$, vs. Fast MoE, 1.7$\times$).

Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45.
